content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'clean/unclean' is understood as ritual-purity language that symbolizes moral and spiritual condition before God: uncleanness represents sin, defilement, and unfitness to approach a holy God, while cleanness represents holiness, moral purity, and acceptable standing in God's presence. Correspondingly, 'cleanse/cleansing' symbolizes God's forgiveness of sin and the sanctification of the believer, accomplished ultimately through the atoning blood of Christ (with the Old Testament washings and purification rites read as types or foreshadowings of that spiritual cleansing). A closely joined sub-theme is Jesus' relocation of defilement from external ritual to the inner heart (Mark 7), and the New Testament's declaration that former ritual categories (foods, Gentiles) are now 'cleansed,' opening covenant access to all peoples.", "primary_basis": ["Leviticus 10:10 (distinguish between the holy and the common, the unclean and the clean)", "Leviticus 11-15 (dietary, disease, and bodily purity laws)", "Psalm 51:2, 7, 10 (wash me, cleanse me with hyssop, create in me a clean heart)", "Psalm 24:3-4 (clean hands and a pure heart)", "Isaiah 1:16-18 (wash yourselves; make yourselves clean; sins white as snow)", "Isaiah 6:5-7 (unclean lips cleansed by the coal from the altar)", "Ezekiel 36:25 (I will sprinkle clean water on you and you shall be clean)", "Zechariah 13:1 (a fountain opened to cleanse from sin and uncleanness)", "Mark 7:14-23 / Matthew 15:10-20 (defilement comes from within; Jesus declares all foods clean)", "Matthew 23:25-26 (cleanse first the inside of the cup)", "Matthew 8:1-4 (Jesus cleanses the leper)", "John 13:10; 15:3 (you are clean because of the word I have spoken)", "Acts 10:9-16, 28 (what God has made clean, do not call common)", "2 Corinthians 7:1 (cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit)", "Ephesians 5:25-27 (cleansing by the washing of water with the word)", "Titus 3:5 (washing of regeneration)", "Hebrews 9:13-14, 22-23; 10:22 (blood of Christ cleansing the conscience; hearts sprinkled clean)", "James 4:8 (cleanse your hands, you sinners; purify your hearts)", "1 John 1:7, 9 (the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Boundary-marker / separation reading: clean-unclean laws primarily functioned to mark Israel off as a distinct, holy people separated from the nations; in the New Testament the abolition of these categories (Acts 10; Ephesians 2) symbolizes the breaking down of the Jew-Gentile barrier and the inclusion of the Gentiles.", "basis": ["Leviticus 20:24-26 (I have separated you from the peoples... you shall therefore make a distinction between clean and unclean)", "Acts 10:9-16, 28, 34-35", "Acts 15:8-9 (cleansed their hearts by faith)", "Ephesians 2:11-22", "Galatians 2:11-14"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Symbolic-order / wholeness reading (associated with Mary Douglas and later anthropological scholarship): purity rules encode a symbolic system of order, wholeness, and conformity to created categories, so that 'unclean' marks anomaly or boundary-crossing rather than sin or hygiene per se.", "basis": ["Genesis 1 (created kinds as the taxonomy underlying Leviticus 11)", "Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 read structurally", "Leviticus 21:17-23 (wholeness/physical integrity and access to the sanctuary)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Death-versus-life symbolism (associated with Jacob Milgrom, Gordon Wenham): sources of impurity (corpses, skin disease, genital discharges, blood loss) cluster around death and the loss of life-force, so uncleanness symbolizes the sphere of death and cleanness the sphere of life and the living God.", "basis": ["Numbers 19 (corpse impurity and the red heifer)", "Leviticus 12-15 (discharges, skin disease as quasi-death; cf. Numbers 12:12)", "Leviticus 17:11 (the life is in the blood)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Strictly ritual/cultic-status reading (common in historical-critical scholarship): in the Old Testament itself, ritual impurity is a non-moral, contagious status governing access to sacred space, distinct from moral impurity generated by sin; the two categories should not be collapsed into a single 'sin' symbolism (Jonathan Klawans and others).", "basis": ["Leviticus 12 (childbirth impurity without any sin)", "Leviticus 15 (normal bodily emissions cause impurity)", "Numbers 19 (corpse contact, an obligatory duty, still defiles)", "Leviticus 18 and Numbers 35:33-34 (moral defilement of the land distinguished from ritual impurity)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Hygienic/health rationale: the clean-unclean food and disease laws were primarily practical public-health provisions, and cleansing rites were proto-sanitary measures; symbolic meaning is secondary.", "basis": ["Leviticus 11 (avoidance of scavengers, pork, shellfish read as health rules)", "Leviticus 13-14 (quarantine of skin disease)", "Deuteronomy 23:12-14 (sanitation in the camp)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Continuing-obligation reading: some groups (e.g., Seventh-day Adventists, Torah-observant/Messianic movements) take the clean-unclean food distinctions as still binding or beneficial, reading Mark 7 and Acts 10 as addressing hand-washing traditions and Gentile inclusion rather than abolishing the dietary categories.", "basis": ["Leviticus 11; Deuteronomy 14", "Acts 10:28 (Peter's own interpretation: about people, not food)", "Isaiah 66:17", "Matthew 5:17-19"], "prominence": "minority"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "There is a broad, recognizable consensus in Christian teaching that clean/unclean symbolizes moral-spiritual purity versus sinful defilement, and that cleansing symbolizes forgiveness and sanctification through Christ, with Old Testament purity rites read typologically (especially via Hebrews 9-10 and 1 John 1). The alternative readings listed are largely explanations of the underlying rationale of the Levitical system (separation, symbolic order, death-life, ritual status, hygiene) and are debated in scholarship; several of them (Douglas, Milgrom/Wenham, Klawans) dominate academic discussion even while the sin-purity symbolism dominates devotional and homiletical use. These layers are often combined rather than treated as mutually exclusive."}
